# Book I, Proposition 3

*A straight line equal to the less, cut off from the greater*

> Given two unequal straight lines, to cut off from the greater a straight line equal to the less.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/03-idea.svg" alt="A circle about the end of the greater straight line, its radius placed equal to the less (blue), cuts off a piece just as long (blue); the rest (red) is left over." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>A circle about the end of the greater straight line, its radius placed equal to the less (blue), cuts off a piece just as long (blue); the rest (red) is left over.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/03.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.3, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let AB, C be the two given unequal straight lines, and let AB be the greater of them.

Thus it is required to cut off from AB the greater a straight line equal to C the less.

At the point A let AD be placed equal to the straight line C; [I. 2]

and with centre A and distance AD let the circle DEF be described. [Post. 3]

Now, since the point A is the centre of the circle DEF,

AE is equal to AD. [Def. 15]

But C is also equal to AD.

Therefore each of the straight lines AE, C is equal to AD; so that AE is also equal to C. [C.N. 1]

Therefore, given the two straight lines AB, C, from AB the greater AE has been cut off equal to C the less.

(Being) what it was required to do.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop03.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop03.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- Given two unequal straight lines, to cut off from the greater a straight line equal to the
less. -/
theorem Prop3 {A B C₁ C₂ : Point} (hC : C₁ ≠ C₂) (h : ‖C₁ C₂‖ < ‖A B‖) :
    ∃ E : Point, Between A E B ∧ ‖A E‖ = ‖C₁ C₂‖ := by
  -- Let AB, C be the two given unequal straight lines, and let AB be the greater of them.
  have hAB : A ≠ B := ne_of_len_gt h
  -- Thus it is required to cut off from AB the greater a straight line equal to C the less.
  -- At the point A let AD be placed equal to the straight line C; [I. 2]
  obtain ⟨D, hAD⟩ := Prop2 A C₁ C₂ hC
  have hAD' : A ≠ D := ne_of_len_eq hAD hC
  -- and with centre A and distance AD let the circle DEF be described. [Post. 3]
  obtain ⟨DEF, hA_DEF, hD_DEF⟩ := Postulate3 A D hAD'
  /- Euclid does not say where the circle DEF meets AB. B lies outside it, since
     AB is the greater, and A, the centre, lies inside; so the straight line AB
     cuts the circle at a point E between A and B (System E, Intersections 4). -/
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
  have hB_out : OutsideCircle B DEF := outside_of_len_gt hA_DEF hD_DEF (by rw [hAD]; exact h)
  obtain ⟨E, hE_DEF, -, hAEB⟩ := line_circle_between (centre_inside hA_DEF) hA_AB hB_out hB_AB
  -- Now, since the point A is the centre of the circle DEF,
  -- AE is equal to AD. [Def. 15]
  have hAE_AD : ‖A E‖ = ‖A D‖ := Definition15 hA_DEF hE_DEF hD_DEF
  -- But C is also equal to AD.
  have hC_AD : ‖C₁ C₂‖ = ‖A D‖ := hAD.symm
  -- Therefore each of the straight lines AE, C is equal to AD; so that AE is also equal to C.
  -- [C.N. 1]
  have hAE_C : ‖A E‖ = ‖C₁ C₂‖ := CommonNotion1 hAE_AD hC_AD
  -- Therefore, given the two straight lines AB, C, from AB the greater AE has been cut off
  -- equal to C the less.
  exact ⟨E, hAEB, hAE_C⟩
  -- (Being) what it was required to do.
```

## Mishnah

**The compass restored.** Euclid now puts I.2 to work. To cut off from AB a straight line equal to C, he places AD equal to C at the point A, by I.2, and lets the circle about A through D do the cutting. With that, the compasses that close of themselves, which Augustus De Morgan pictures under I.2, can do all that an ordinary pair does: carry a length and lay it off along a straight line.

**Eight figures, or one?** Proclus again finds many cases, eight figures in all. Heath remarks that he gets them only "by practically incorporating the construction of the preceding proposition, instead of assuming it as we are entitled to do. If Prop. 2 is assumed, there is really only one 'case' of the present proposition" (vol. 1, p. 247). In Lean, citing I.2 is exactly assuming it: we use `Prop2` as a finished result, whatever its own figure looked like. Heath also sets aside Robert Potts' two cases, cutting from one end of AB or the other, and Lean agrees: when I.6 cuts from the end B, it simply cites `Prop3` with the letters exchanged.

**Why should the circle cut AB?** Euclid simply takes E where the circle DEF meets AB. Why should it meet AB at all, and between A and B? The centre A is inside the circle and B, farther from A than the radius, is outside; a straight line from inside a circle to outside crosses it (System E, Intersections 4). Lean must say so, and must first name the straight line AB, as in I.1. Our `Prop3` keeps E between A and B, as cutting off from AB means, for I.5 and I.6 rely on it. Euclid names the less straight line by one letter, C; Lean, which knows a finite straight line only by its two ends, gives C a pair of them.

**The modern way.** E is the point a known fraction of the way along AB: E = A + (|C| / |AB|)(B − A), where |C| is the length of C.

## Further reading

- For E as a point a known fraction of the way along AB, Kiran S. Kedlaya's [*Geometry Unbound*](https://kskedlaya.org/geometryunbound/) (2006, free online), ch. 2, "Algebraic methods", a lively book that sets vectors and complex numbers beside classical proofs.
- For what a straightedge and compass can do, now that I.2 and I.3 have given the compass its full power, John Stillwell's [*The Four Pillars of Geometry*](https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-29052-4) (2005), ch. 1, "Straightedge and compass", a short, clear book that looks at the plane four ways.
